cards.title: Introduction to Messaging Architecture
cards.content:
Asynchronous messaging allows microservices to communicate decoupled from one another. Spring Boot provides unified abstractions for various messaging backends including JMS, AMQP (RabbitMQ), and Apache Kafka.

  • Decoupling: Producers and consumers operate independently.
  • Scalability: Queue workloads can be distributed across multiple instances.
  • Resilience: Messages persist until processed, ensuring data safety.

cards.title: Spring JMS Integration
cards.content:
Spring Boot simplifies Java Message Service (JMS) with starter dependencies and auto-configuration using JmsTemplate and @JmsListener.

@Service
public class MessageProducer {
    @Autowired
    private JmsTemplate jmsTemplate;

    public void send(String queue, String message) {
        jmsTemplate.convertAndSend(queue, message);
    }
}

cards.title: AMQP & RabbitMQ Concepts
cards.content:
RabbitMQ uses the Advanced Message Queuing Protocol (AMQP). Messages are sent to Exchanges, which route them to Queues based on Bindings and Routing Keys.

Spring AMQP provides RabbitTemplate for publishing and @RabbitListener for receiving messages asynchronously.

Buffer that stores messages until consumed
Link between an exchange and a queue
Attributes evaluated to route message to specific queue

cards.title: Apache Kafka Integration
cards.content:
Apache Kafka is a distributed event-streaming platform. Unlike traditional brokers, Kafka relies on an immutable partitioned commit log.

@Component
public class KafkaConsumer {
    @KafkaListener(topics = "orders", groupId = "order-group")
    public void listen(String message) {
        System.out.println("Received: " + message);
    }
}
